## Abstract

The abstract (1) states the nature of the investigation and (2) summarizes the important conclusions. The abstract should be suitable for indexing. Your abstract should:

  - Be set as a single paragraph.
  - Be less than 250 words for all journals except GRL, for which the limit is 150 words.
  - Not include table or figure mentions.
  - Avoid reference citations unless dependent on or directly related to another paper (e.g., companion, comment, reply, or commentary on another paper(s)). AGU’s Style Guide discusses formatting citations in abstracts.
  - Define all abbreviations.


## plain-language-summary

A Plain Language Summary (PLS) can be an incredibly effective science communication tool. By summarizing your paper in non-technical terms, you can explain your research and its relevance to a much broader audience. A PLS is required for submissions to AGU Advances, G-Cubed, GeoHealth, GRL, JAMES, JGR: Biogeosciences, JGR: Oceans, JGR: Planets, JGR: Solid Earth, JGR: Atmospheres, Space Weather, and Reviews of Geophysics, but optional for other journals.  A PLS should be no longer than 200 words and should be free of jargon, acronyms, equations, and any technical information that would be unknown to people from outside your scientific discipline. Read our tips for creating an effective PLS.

## Results

* Description of the conceptual model + equations

### Simple model of sea ice growth 

I start with a simplified model of sea ice growth.
In this model, each cell has an area of water and of an area covered with ice. 
Assuming that sea ice is a perfect insulator, the ocean surface exchanges heat with the atmosphere only in the ice-free surface. 
This heat flux is parameterised with a bulk formula with a constant exchange coefficient and sea surface temperature is assumed to be constant and equal to the freezing point. 
This latter assumption is somewhat justified by the fact that a mixture of water and ice in thermodynamic equilibrium will stay at the freezing point, and any heat gain or loss will either melt or freeze more ice.

The full formula for the heat exchange per unit area then is 

$$
F = \alpha (T_a - T_f) (1 - I_a)
$$ {#eq-flux}

Where, $T_f$ and $T_a$ are the freezing point temperature of the ocean and the atmosphere respectively, $I_a$ is the proportion of the gridcell covered with ice and $\alpha$ is a proportionality constant. 

The change in sea ice concentration will be related to $F$. 
To transform the heat exchange flux to a proportion of sea ice melted or ice-free ocean frozen $F_{p}$, we use this transformation. 

$$
F_{p} = \frac{F} {(1 + \left| F \right |)}
$$

This transformation ensures that $F_p$ is bounded by $\left(0, 1\right)$ and parameterises a saturation point beyond extremely strong fluxes will be partially counteracted by other processes like horizontal and vertical transport of heat within the top layer of the ocean. 

If $F$ is negative, the heat lost to the ocean is balanced by freezing. 
However, because only ice-free areas can freeze, I assume that the change in sea ice concentration is also proportial to the ice-free area. 

$$
\dot{I} = -\beta_f F_{p} (1 - I_a)
$$

Where $\beta_f$ is a freezing proportionality constant. 

Conversely, if $F$ is positive, the ocean gains heat which is used to melt ice. 
In this case it is only ice-covered areas which can melt, making the change in sea ice concentration proportional to sea ice concentration itself.

$$
\dot{I} = -\beta_m F_{p} I_a
$$

Where $\beta_m$ is a memlting proportionality constant that in principle could be different from $\beta_f$. 

The full model, therefore is

$$
\dot{I} =
\begin{cases}
\frac{-\beta_f \alpha (T_a - T_f) (1 - I_a)^2 }{ 1 + \alpha (T_a - T_f) (1 - I_a)}    &  T_a \le T_f, \\
\frac{-\beta_m \alpha (T_a - T_f) (1 - I_a) I_a }{ 1 + \alpha (T_a - T_f) (1 - I_a)}  &  T_a 	> T_f
\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-model}

```{r}
#| label: model_monthly

model_monthly <- loess(
  daice ~ t2m + aice,
  data = grid_monthly[n > 50],
  span = 0.1,
  degree = 2
)

# Observed t2m range at each COARSE aice value actually present in grid_monthly
data_range <- grid_monthly[n > 100] |>
  _[, .(t2m_min = min(t2m), t2m_max = max(t2m)), by = .(aice)]
setkey(data_range, aice)


t2m_seq <- seq(-70, 30, by = 0.1)
aice_seq <- seq(0, 1, by = 0.01)

smooth_grid <- CJ(t2m = t2m_seq, aice = aice_seq)

setkey(smooth_grid, aice)

# # Roll-join: for each fine aice value, borrow the nearest coarse bin's
# # observed t2m range
smooth_grid <- data_range[smooth_grid, roll = "nearest"]


spmax <- function(x, y, e = 0.001) {
  (x + y + sqrt((x - y)^2 + e)) / 2
}

spmin <- function(x, y, e = 0.001) {
  (x + y - sqrt((x - y)^2 + e)) / 2
}

clamp_daice <- function(daice, aice) {
  pmax(-aice, pmin(daice, 1 - aice))
}

smooth_grid[, t2m_clamped := pmax(t2m_min, pmin(t2m, t2m_max))]


smooth_grid[,
  daice := predict(
    model_monthly,
    newdata = data.frame(aice = aice, t2m = t2m_clamped)
  )
] |>
  _[t2m > 0 & daice > 0, daice := -daice]

smooth_grid[aice == 0, daice := smooth_grid[aice == 0.01, daice]]

smooth_grid[, daice := clamp_daice(daice, aice)]

b <- seq(-1, 1, by = 0.1)
```

```{r}
#| label: tf_model
zero <- purrr::possibly(
  function(x, y) {
    approxfun(x, y) |>
      uniroot(interval = c(min(x), max(x))) |>
      _$root
  },
  otherwise = NA_real_
)


tf <- grid_monthly[n > 10 & t2m %between% c(-15, 1)] |>
  _[, .(y = zero(t2m, daice)), by = .(x = aice)]


tf_model <- lm(y ~ poly(x, degree = 4, raw = TRUE), data = tf)
```

```{r}
#| label: models
daice_fitted <- function(mod, aice, t2m) {
  predict(mod, newdata = data.frame(aice = aice, t2m = t2m))
}

high_t <- -1
low_t <- -7

celsius <- \(x) paste0(x, "°C")

aice_value <- function(t2m_range, max = 1) {
  function(t2m) {
    midpoint <- min(t2m_range)
    r <- diff(range(t2m_range))

    zeros <- midpoint + c(-r, r)
    max_value <- ((midpoint - zeros[1]) * (midpoint - zeros[2]))

    val <- (t2m - zeros[1]) * (t2m - zeros[2]) / max_value * max

    val <- ifelse(t2m < midpoint, max, val)
    ifelse(t2m > max(zeros), 0, val)
  }
}

labs_models <- c(
  daice = "Obs",
  daice_simple = "Simple model",
  daice_tf = "Variable T_f",
  daice_gamma = "Model with extra flux",
  daice_poly = "Polynomial fit"
)

smooth_grid_coarse <- smooth_grid[, .(
  t2m,
  aice,
  value = daice,
  variable = "daice_poly"
)] |>
  _[,
    Interpolate(
      value ~ t2m + aice,
      x.out = unique(grid_monthly$t2m),
      y.out = unique(grid_monthly$aice)
    ),
    by = variable
  ]

models <- grid_monthly |>
  _[, .(t2m, aice, daice, n)] |>
  _[,
    let(
      daice_simple = daice_fitted(mod_simple, aice, t2m),
      daice_gamma = daice_fitted(mod_gamma, aice, t2m),
      # daice_damping = daice_fitted(mod_damping, aice, t2m),
      # daice_poly = predict(model_monthly, newdata = .SD),
      daice_tf = daice_fitted(mod_tf, aice, t2m)
    )
  ] |>
  # _[,
  #   daice_damping := daice_simple *
  #     0.8 -
  #     0.5 * (aice - aice_value(c(-20, 0), 0.8)(t2m))
  # ] |>
  _[, n := NULL] |>
  melt(
    id.vars = c("aice", "t2m")
  ) |>
  rbind(smooth_grid_coarse) |>
  _[, variable := factor(variable, levels = names(labs_models))]
```

To illustrate the basic properties of this simple model, @fig-aice-lines (dashed lines) shows the change in monthly sea ice concentration change as function of sea ice concentration for one temperature in the melting and freezing regimes. 
The parameters were fitted to observations using non-linear least squares. 
For a given temperature below freezing, sea ice growth is maximum at low sea ice concentrations since that maximises both the heat loss and ice-free ocean that is available for freezing. 
At high sea ice concentrations heat fluxes are suppressed and there is little open water to freeze, leading to slow growth. 
At a given temperature above freezing, on the other hand, sea ice melt is slow at low concentrations because there is little ice left to melt and at high concentrations because the ice insulates the ocean from the atmosphere. 
Maximum melt is at around 75% sea ice concentrations, when there is enough ice to melt and enough ice-free ocean for the ocean to exchange heat.

We can compare this model with observed values, computed by averaging gridcells with temperatures of `r celsius(low_t)` and `r celsius(high_t)` $\pm$ 0.25°C and sea ice concentration values binned at boxes 2% wide (solid lines in @fig-aice-lines). 
The overall curve in observations fits notably well with the simple theory in the melt regime. 
Melt is zero at zero concentrations by mathematical necessity, but it is also low at high concentrations, showing the stabilisation effect of sea ice insulation. 
At 100% sea ice concentrations, melt values are not exactly zero. 
This in likely partly due to the binning -- which means that these values are actually the average of values between 95% and 100% -- but also likely a real effect that includes many processes that the model doesn't take into account, such as transport, deformation, melting from below and heat exchange through the ice itself. 

In the growth regime, observations follow the simple model roughly; with low growth at high concentrations and high growth at low concentrations. 
However, it deviates from the model in two significant ways. 
First, at sea ice concentrations lower than 25%, growth starts to flatten out.
This could be due to missing processes, but it is also important to note that satellite observations are increasingly uncertain below ~15% and that there is no data between 0% and 10% concentrations. 
Second, at high concentrations sea ice actually melts even when exposed to low temperatures. 

A more complete picture of the problem is shown in @fig-daice-monthly which shows observed average sea ice concentration change as a function of monthly sea ice concentrations and 2-metre temperature.
The black line estimates the "zero line" that divides sea ice growth from melt. 
Thi is essentially an estimate of the effective $T_f$ in @eq-flux. 
Contraty to the model's assumptiont, this zero line is not constant and instead depends heavily on sea ice concentration. 
At low concentrations, air temperatures just below -2°C are enough to cause sea ice growth on average, but as sea ice concentrations rise, the air needs to be increasingly colder for ice not to melt. 
At about 50% sea ice concentration, air temperatures need to be lower than -5°C for ice to grow. 
This property cannot be captured by the model in @eq-model, which assumes that sea ice will grow whenever air temperature is below the freezing point of ocean water, whose dependency with salinity is nowhere near as strong. 

One possible problem could be the assumption that ocean temperatures are constant. 
However, reproducing the same plot but using the difference between 2-metre air temperature and SST results in almost the same relationship (@fig-daice-monthly-sst).



```{r}
#| label: fig-daice-monthly-sst
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-cap: Same as @fig-daice-monthly but using the difference between 2-metre temperature and SST. 

plot_daice_monthly2 <- plot_daice_monthly

plot_daice_monthly2@layers <- plot_daice_monthly2@layers[1:4]
plot_daice_monthly2@scales$scales[[
  3
]]$name <- "Difference between\n2-metre temperature and SST (°C)"

plot_daice_monthly2 +
  (daice |>
    _[!is.na(daice)] |>
    _[,
      .(value = mean(daice), n = sum(!is.na(daice))),
      by = .(
        t2m = cut_mid(t2m - sst, 0.2, 0),
        aice = cut_mid(aice, 0.01, 0.11)
      )
    ]) +
  facet_null()
```

A direct refinement of the model is to postulate an ad-hoc dependency of $T_f$ on sea ice concentration. 
The black line in @fig-daice-monthly is well modelled a fourth degree polinomial in @eq-tf-model fitted by linear regression. 

```{r}
#| output: asis
#| label: eq-tf-model
coefmodel <- coef(tf_model)
powers <- seq_along(coefmodel) - 1

term <- ifelse(powers != 0, "I", "")
power <- ifelse(powers > 1, paste0("^", powers), "")
term <- paste0(term, power)

sign <- ifelse(sign(coefmodel) < 0, "-", "+")
number <- scales::number(abs(coefmodel))

term <- paste0(number, term)

term <- paste(sign, term)

rhs <- paste0(term, collapse = " ")

cat(paste0("$$\nT_f = ", rhs, "\n$$ {#eq-tf-model}"))
```

This model reproduces the dependency of $T_f$ on sea ice concentration by definition (@fig-aice-lines c), and matches the overall shape relatively well (@fig-daice-monthly c).
However, it slightly overestimates the melt ocurring at low temperatures at high sea ice concentrations and features a discontinuity in the derivative of $dI/dt$ with respect to sea ice concentration, creating a "kink" seen in @fig-aice-lines c. 
Moreover, this is a wholelly ad-hoc modification. 
Regardless of goodness-of-fit, it would be preferrable to have a model in which the dependency of  $T_f$ with sea ice concentration arised as an emergent property from physically motivated rules. 

A physics-based refinement of the model is pressupose a positive heat flux representing warming of the water from the bottom by mixing of relatively warmer subsurface water. 
Under this formulation, ice would grow only if the freezing at the surface from the atmosphere was larger than the melting from the ocean, which would require more extreme air temperature when ice insulation is higher at higher concentrations, thus creating an effective dependency on $T_f$ on sea ice concentration. 
Both wind forcing and waves can induce mixing, and both are dampened by the presence of sea ice, therefore this flux should also be proportional to the ice-free area.

In this full model the change in sea ice concentration is decomposed into change due to air fluxes and ocean fluxes. 

$$
\dot{I} = \dot{I}\Bigg|_a  + \dot{I}\Bigg|_o 
$$

Where $\dot{I}\Bigg|_a$ is computed as before and $\dot{I}\Bigg|_o$ is 

$$
\dot{I}\Bigg|_o = \beta_m F_o I 
$$

Where $F_o = \gamma(1 - I)$. 

The results of this model are shown in @fig-aice-lines d and @fig-daice-monthly d.
This model produces a $T_f$ dependency comparable with observations, although the exact shape is clearly not correct; it is too flat at low sea ice concentrations and too steep at high sea ice concentrations. 
Nevertheless, it suggest that ocean processes might be responsible for this phenomenon. 

An alternative model imposing a damping forcing that relaxes sea ice concentrations towards a temperature-dependent value were tried. 
This tries to simulate that gridpoints with either particularly high or low sea ice concentration values compared with their surroundings will tend to either export ice away or gain ice from their neighbours. 
However, the estimated damping strength from observations was minimal and could not explain the observed shaped of the ice-temperature surface. 
A nudge would also not be compatible with the observed zero melt at 100% sea ice concentration. 




* Integration of the model

Even a perfect fit to the observed average relationship will only capture a fracton of the total variabilty of sea ice, since it ignores a multitude of external factors and internal sea ice proceses. 
To explore how much can be explained, we integrate the models in time using 2-metre temperature fields from ERA5 as forcing.

```{r}
#| label: forcing_temp
#| cache: false
time_translate <- data.table(
  time = seq(
    as.Date(min(daice[!is.na(aice)]$time)),
    as.Date(max(daice[!is.na(aice)]$time)),
    by = "1 month"
  )
) |>
  _[, t := 0:(.N - 1)]

time_fun <- \(t) {
  as.Date(as.POSIXct(
    approxfun(time_translate$t, time_translate$time)(t),
    tz = "UTC"
  ))
}
forcing_temp <- era_temp_fun(daice[mask, on = c("x", "y")])
```

```{r}
Sys.setenv(PKG_CXXFLAGS = "-O3 -march=native -fopenmp")

Rcpp::sourceCpp(here::here("src/lookup.cpp"))
```

```{r}
#| label: d_aice
d_ice <- function(grid) {
  if (anyNA(grid)) {
    stop("Missing values in grid")
  }

  function(state, time, forcing) {
    t2m <- forcing(time)
    d_ice <- lookup(state, t2m, grid)
    d_ice
  }
}


make_grid_matrix <- function(grid) {
  daice_grid <- dcast(grid, aice ~ t2m, value.var = "daice")[, -1] |>
    as.matrix()
  return(daice_grid)
}

lm_to_dice <- function(model) {
  smooth_grid |>
    copy() |>
    _[, daice := clamp_daice(predict(model, .SD), aice)] |>
    make_grid_matrix() |>
    d_ice()
}
```

```{r}
#| label: d_aice-models
models <- list(
  model_obs = d_ice(make_grid_matrix(smooth_grid)),
  mod_simple = lm_to_dice(mod_simple)
)
```

```{r}
#| label: simulate_model
simulate_model <- function(model) {
  sample <- model(stat = start$aice, time = 0, forcing = forcing_temp)
  hash <- digest::digest(sample, algo = "xxh3_128")
  out <- glue::glue("data/derived/simulations/{hash}.nc")

  if (file.exists(out)) {
    message("Returning cached result")
    return(out)
  }

  sim <- evolve(
    start = start,
    model = model,
    start_time = min(time_translate$t),
    end_time = max(time_translate$t),
    dt = 1 / 31,
    forcing = forcing_temp
  )
  sim <- time_translate[sim, on = "t"][, t := NULL]

  sim |>
    tidyr::complete(time, x, y) |>
    data.table::setDT() |>
    _[order(time, -y, x)] |>
    metR:::WriteNetCDF(
      tempfile(),
      "aice",
      c("x", "y", "time"),
      order = FALSE
    ) |>
    rcdo::cdo_setgrid(CDRv6()) |>
    rcdo::cdo_execute(out = out)
}
```

```{r}
#| label: sims
sims <- lapply(models, simulate_model) |>
  c(list(obs = CDRv6(), s2 = s2()))

sims <- data.table(model = names(sims), file = unlist(sims))
```

```{r}
  _[n > 10 & i.n > 10] |>

  experiment == "historical",
  .(model, rmse = estimate)
] |>

model_order <- function(model) {
  factor(model, levels = rmse_factor$model)
}

cmip_grid[, model := model_order(model)]
cmip_grid_split[, model := model_order(model)]
```
